post.caption: Git saves a full snapshot of your project on every commit and stays small by naming every file after a hash of its content. (Pack files add delta compression on top, but the model is snapshots.)

scenes.title: Git doesn't store your *changes.*
scenes.narration: Git doesn't store your changes. It stores snapshots of your whole project, and it's still tiny. Here's how.

scenes.heading: How do you version files?
scenes.narration: Older tools stored diffs, so getting an old version meant replaying changes. Git stores a full snapshot for every commit instead.

scenes.text: A full snapshot every commit sounds ==huge.==
scenes.sub: It isn't, thanks to one trick.
scenes.narration: A full snapshot every commit sounds huge. It isn't, thanks to one trick.

scenes.heading: Everything is named by its *content*
scenes.narration: Every file is stored as a blob, named by a hash of its contents. A commit points to a tree, and trees point to blobs and other trees.
Try it. Cat-file on HEAD shows a commit pointing at its tree. Ask for the tree, and you get blobs and folders, each with a hash.
So when you change one file and commit, only that file gets a new blob. The folders above it get new trees. Everything else is reused by its hash.

scenes.label: hex characters name every object
scenes.sub: Same content, same name. Stored once.
scenes.narration: Each name is a forty character hash. Same content, same name, so identical files are stored once.

scenes.heading: Snapshots by hash give you
scenes.narration: That's why checkout is fast, duplicate files are free, and corrupted data gets caught, because every hash is checked.

scenes.title: Snapshots, ==not diffs.==
scenes.narration: Snapshots, not diffs. Follow for more.
